records.heading: Q: Is there any difference on reactivities of branched and linear sulfonyl hydrazide in the
alkenylation?
records.text:
A: We have tried alkenylation with primary sulfonyl hydrazide (branched and linear) to synthesize
compound 34 and its analogue (one carbon less). It was demonstrated that branched sulfonyl hydrazide
affords higher yield.

records.heading: Q: Are there any indicative phenomenon changes during the alkenylation of alkynylation
reaction?
records.text:
A: Usually, we would observe suspension after all materials dissolved in DMF at room temperature and
stirred for several minutes, but it was not detrimental for this reaction yield. Also, the suspension will
become clear after heating for a while (ca. 10-30 minutes). Besides, in the alkynylation, the color of
reaction crude will be dark red while the color of alkenylation will turn yellow or green.

records.heading: Q: I am trying to prepare hydrazide from the reduction of hydrazone with NaBH, but I am having
records.text:
trouble with insufficient conversion. What should I do?
A: During the reduction of hydrazone with NaBH4, maintaining a temperature of 0°C is essential to
inhibit the formation of by-products. However, a solid is often observed forming during the reaction.
We suggest increasing the solvent volume, using more equivalent of NaBH4, and extending the reaction
time to improve conversion. If the conversion is still incomplete, purification by silica gel
chromatography and recrystallization may be required. Additionally, we found that residual hydrazone
in the crude product does not affect reactivity.
38 4. User guide for selecting conditions and starting materials The user guide is presented based on currently available data separated for transformations. However, this user guide is subject to change as more data becomes available.
1. Pempidine as the base (instead of Et3N) usually gives higher yields in the arylation protocols.
2. dNH2-bpy usually gives higher yields over dtbbpy in the arylation protocols and is more general in
terms of (hetero)aryl (pseudo)halide scope. dNH2-bpy is necessary for alkenylation and alkynylation.
3. The hydrazone arylation protocol is best suited for quick library synthesis, whereas the hydrazide
arylation protocol usually gives higher yields and affords a cleaner reaction mixture profile.
4. Et3N gives slightly higher yield in the alkenylation and alkynylation reactions.
5. ArOTf’s currently only work in the hydrazone coupling as shown in the scope. Comparing with the
corresponding hydrazide coupling, the yield drops to only around 10% (NMR). We postulate that the
decomposition rate of the hydrazide is to high, thus not matching the oxidative addition rate well in the
hydrazide coupling, whereas the hydrazone needs to be reduced which allows the coupling to occur.
6. Linear Ts hydrazides isomers are generally more stable than 3,5-difluorophenylsulfonyl hydrazides.
Both are competent in the arylation reaction and alkenylation. Linear Ts hydrazides lead to low yields
in trifluoromethylation and alkylation. In terms of alkylation, best yields are obtaining using 3,5-
difluorophenylsulfonyl hydrazides. Similarly, trifluoromethylation works well with 3,5-
difluorophenylsulfonyl hydrazides but it’s also compatible with branched Ts hydrazides.

4 2. Synthetic Procedures 2.1 General Procedure A: Synthesis of unsubstituted sulfonyl hydrazides The sulfonyl chloride (1.0 equiv., 20 mmol) was added to a round-bottom flask under air. The flask was evacuated then backfilled with an inert gas 3 times (Ar or N2). Next, dry THF (30 ml) was added, then the solution was cooled to 0 °C using an ice bath. Once at 0 °C (wait at least 10 min to make sure it’s at 0 °C, but no more than 15 min, because it’s not stable over extended times), aqueous hydrazine hydrate solution 50-60% [assumed 55 m/m%] (2.5 equiv., 50 mmol, 2909 mg, 2.83 ml) was added dropwise. The formation of hydrazine hydrochloride, a white precipitate, was immediately observed. The reaction mixture was kept at 0 °C after addition of the hydrazine until complete consumption of the sulfonyl chloride was observed (typically < 30 min, checked by TLC 30% EtOAc in hexanes). Note: in the unlikely case the reaction stalls, it can be warmed to room temperature.
However, these activated products can slowly hydrolyse and decompose under the reaction conditions,
thus close monitoring at room temperature is necessary.
After complete consumption of the sulfonyl chloride, EtOAc (70 ml) was added at 0 °C. The
cold reaction mixture was then transferred to a separatory funnel and washed repeatedly with brine (5
× 70 ml) in order to remove any excess hydrazine. Note: the mixture can warm up to room temperature
during workup after the addition of the organic phase, EtOAc. The organic phase was dried over
MgSO4, filtered, then evaporated, thus yielding the title sulfonyl hydrazides as a white crystalline solid
(typically > 80% yield).
Notes: 1. The starting sulfonyl chlorides are highly crystalline solids, but sometimes supplied as orange
crystals. The 3,5-diF sulfonyl chloride can be recrystallised from hexanes (15 g sulfonyl chloride in 30
ml hexanes) using a hot filtration to remove most of the orange impurities. 2. All sulfonyl hydrazides
made during this work were obtained as white solids. In case the product’s purity in not satisfactory
(this can mainly happen due to impure sulfonyl chlorides starting materials), it can be purified by
column chromatography. In the case of the 3,5-diF sulfonyl hydrazide it was columned using 30%
EtOAc in hexanes. 3. As a precaution, the hydrazides were kept in the freezer for long-term storage.
5 2.2 General Procedure B: Synthesis of sulfonyl hydrazones In a round bottom flask, the ketone (1.0 equiv., 5.0 mmol) was dissolved in dry MeOH (10 ml) under air. Note: it’s important to completely dissolve the ketone as the product my precipitate out! Next, the sulfonyl hydrazide (1.0 equiv., 5.0 mmol) was added in a single portion as a solid which is quickly dissolved in the reaction mixture. The hydrazone product sometime precipitates within 5 to 30 minutes.
Note: in other cases, the product does not precipitate, please see below. The reaction mixture was
stirred for 30 min to ensure complete formation of the product, then filtered. The solid product was
washed with pentanes (3 × 35 ml), then dried under vacuum to afford the activated ketones (typically >
80% yield).
In case the product didn’t precipitate from the reaction mixture after full consumption of the
starting materials (usually < 30 min), the reaction mixture was evaporated to complete dryness yielding
a sticky solid/gum. Pentane (50 ml) was added and the solid was sonicated for 30 min to turn the
hydrazones into white powders. The slurry was filtered and washed with pentane (3 × 35 ml), then dried
under vacuum to afford the activated ketones (typically > 95% yield).
In case the activated ketones are not clean (because the reaction doesn’t go to competition so
there’s leftover ketone and/or hydrazide) they can be recrystallised or purified by normal and/or reverse
phase flash column chromatography. Recrystallisation was usually done by dissolving the crude in
minimal amount of EtOAc (2-3 ml), then pentane (100 ml) was added to crash out the product.
6 2.3 General Procedure C: Cross-coupling of sulfonyl hydrazones and (hetero)aryl halides via in situ generated hydrazides To a long tube a stirrer bar, the sulfonyl hydrazone (1.0 equiv., 0.50 mmol), the (hetero)aryl halide (if solid, 1.5 equiv., 0.75 mmol), Ni(dme)Cl2 (20 mol%, 0.1 mmol, 22.0 mg), and dNH2-bpy (20 mol%, 0.1 mmol, 18.6 mg) were added. The vial was capped with a septa cap, then evacuated and backfilled with an inert gas (Ar or N2) three times. Dry DMF (2.5 ml) was added, followed by the (hetero)aryl halide (if liquid, 1.5 equiv., 0.75 mmol), then the mixture was stirred (700 rpm) at room temperature for 3-5 min to dissolve all the solids. Note: the colour of the mixture is dependent mostly on the colour of the aryl halide as the nickel complex is almost colourless. Next, while stirring, PhSiMe2H (3.0 equiv., 1.5 mmol, 204.5 mg, 230 μl) and pempidine (3.0 equiv., 1.5 mmol, 233.0 mg, 272 μl) were added. Note: there might be slight colour change to a darker shade after the addition of the base. However, in some cases a solid is formed which is a potential indicator that the coupling will not work due to the strong coordination of the substrate to nickel. That being said, there were coupling reactions where a solid was formed yet we isolated the product in good yield. The reaction mixture was again stirred at room temperature to achieve a homogenous solution (usually less than 2 min), the septa cap was quickly replaced with a solid cap, then it was secured with a layer of electrical tape. The reaction was transferred to a stirred (700 rpm), pre-heated oil bath at 75 °C and stirred overnight (16 to 18 hours) at 700 rpm. Notes: 1. We highly recommend the use of a well-stirred oil bath to achieve efficient heat transfer. Sand baths and other alternatives did not prove to be effective, because they do not reliably heat the reaction to 75 °C. Furthermore, it is highly recommended that the level of the solvent in the vial is below the level of the oil in the bath. 2. We do not recommend sampling the reaction before the indicated time has passed as it can disturb the catalytic system and inadvertently quench the reaction prematurely. 3. The reaction develops N2 gas, thus the vial becomes slightly pressurised over the course of the reaction. The reaction mixture was transferred to a vial and the volatiles and DMF were evaporated under reduced pressure. EtOAc (15 ml) was added, then it was washed with saturated Rochelle’s salt solution (15 ml) to remove the inorganic salts. The phases were separated, the aqueous phase was washed with EtOAc (2 × 10 ml), then the organic phases were combined, dried, and evaporated to yield the crude product. Note: in case there’s a significant amount of DMF left, the crude can be taken up in EtOAc (25 ml) and washed with 10 m/m% aqueous LiCl solution (2 × 10 ml) to remove DMF. The crude product was purified by normal or reversed-phase column chromatography on silica gel to give the cross-coupled product.

11 2.5 General Procedure E: Reduction of sulfonyl hydrazones to alkyl sulfonyl hydrazides In a round bottom flask, the sulfonyl hydrazone (prepared as described above, General Procedure B, 10 mmol) was dissolved in CH2Cl2 (25 ml) and MeOH (25 ml), then the mixture was cooled to 0 °C. At 0 °C, NaBH4 (2.0 equiv.) was added portionwise. Note: significant H2 gas formation was observed, hence the portionwise addition of the solid. The reaction was stirred at 0 °C for 1 h. If, at this point, the reaction didn’t go to completion more equivalents of NaBH4 were added (1.0 equiv.
every 30 min) until complete conversion (usually stalls around 95%) was observed. Note: it is important
to keep the reaction mixture at 0 °C to suppress side-product formation. Once the reaction has reached
the desired conversion, the mixture was quenched with sat. aq. NH4Cl solution (100 ml) and the aqueous
phase was extracted with EtOAc (3 × 100 ml; alternatively, CH2Cl2 can also be used). The organic
phase was dried, evaporated thus yielding the hydrazide with sufficient purity for cross-coupling. The
hydrazides can be purified by column chromatography if necessary. Note: in our experience, many of
these hydrazides have limited stability in solution, but they are bench stable as isolated solids. So, it is
not necessary to use them immediately in a subsequent reaction, but it is important not to leave the
reduction reaction stirring overnight.

36 3. Frequently asked questions Q: Are hydrazones bench stable?
A: Hydrazones (both tosyl and sulfonyl 3,5-dF-Ph) are stable solid and have been stored on the bench
for months.
Q: Are hydrazides bench stable?
A: The majority of 2°-cyclic sulfonyl hydrazides are bench stable solids, particularly in the case of tosyl
hydrazides. 2°-acyclic and 1°-tosyl hydrazides obtained after hydrazone reduction should be used
shortly after preparation whereas 1° hydrazides prepared through Mitsunobu (different NSO2Ar
regioisomer) are more stable (several days on a benchtop).
Q: What are the major by-products and side-products observed in each reaction?
A: In the case of arylation using sulfonyl hydrazones, as with many cross-coupling reactions, proto-
dehalogenation, halogen exchange of aryl bromides to aryl chlorides, and homo-coupling of the aryl
unit have been observed. The hydrazide arylation is usually a very clean reaction. Sulfur containing
cross-coupled compounds have been observed such as the ones depicted below in varying quantities in
both arylation reactions. The primary by-products of the trifluoromethylation are olefin and alkene
products. For Giese addition and alkylation protonation and dimerization of the hydrazide are the major
side products.

quenched with saturated NH4Cl solution (3 mL) and extracted with diethyl ether (1.5 mL) four times.

To a long tube a stirrer bar, Ticagrelor (1.0 equiv., 0.1 mmol, 52.2 mg) and PPh3 (3.5 equiv., 0.35 mmol,
91.8 mg) were added. The vial was capped with a septa cap, then evacuated and backfilled with an inert
gas (Ar or N2) three times. Dry THF (1 ml) was added, then the mixture was cooled to 0 °C. At 0 °C,
diisopropyl azodicarboxylate (DIAD, 3.5 equiv. 0.35 mmol, 70.8 mg, 69 µl) was added dropwise, after
stirring for 10 min at 0 °C, p-Toluenesulfonyl hydrazide (TsNHNH2, 4.0 equiv., 0.40 mmol, 74.5 mg)
was added as a solid, then the reaction mixture was stirred at 0 °C for 4 hours. After the reaction was
complete (as detected by LCMS), sat. aq. NH4Cl (1.0 ml) was added to the mixture, and the aqueous
layer was extracted with EtOAc (3 × 3 ml), then the organic phases were combined, washed with brine
51 (3 ml) dried, and evaporated to yield the crude activated product. The crude product was transferred to a new long tube and a stirrer bar was added followed by 5-bromo-2-(trifluoromethyl)pyridine (93, 2.0 equiv., 0.20 mmol, 45.0 mg), Ni(dme)Cl2 (30 mol%, 0.03 mmol, 6.6 mg), and dtbbpy (30 mol%, 0.03 mmol, 6.6 mg). The vial was capped with a septa cap, then evacuated and backfilled with an inert gas (Ar or N2) three times. Dry, degassed DMF (1 ml) was added, and the mixture was stirred at room temperature until all solids dissolved, then Et3N (3.0 equiv., 0.3 mmol, 30.4 mg, 42 µl) was added and the cap was secured with electrical tape. The reaction was transferred to a stirred (700 rpm), pre-heated oil bath at 60 °C and stirred for 8 hours. Next, sat. aq. NH4Cl (1.0 ml) was added to the mixture, the phases were separated, the aqueous phase was washed with EtOAc (3 × 3 ml), then the organic phases were combined, dried, and evaporated to yield the crude product. The crude product was purified by preparative thin-layer chromatography giving the title compound in 33% yield (21.5 mg, 0.033 mmol).
